source_text: Hic ergo scelestissimi illi provocant quaestiones. Adeo, dicunt, Baptismus non est necessarius, quibus fides satis est, nam et Abraham nullius aquae nisi fidei sacramento Deo placuit. Sed in omnibus posteriora concludunt, et sequentia antecedentibus praevalent. Fuerit salus retro per fidem nudam ante Domini passionem et resurrectionem. At ubi fides aucta est credendi in nativitatem, passionem, resurrectionemque ejus, addita est ampliatio sacramento, obsignatio Baptismi vestimentum quodammodo fidei, quae retro erat nuda, nec potentiam habuit sine sua lege. Lex enim tinguendi imposita est, et forma praescripta. Ite, inquit, docete nationes, tinguentes eas in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti. Huic legi collata definitio illa: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu, non intrabit in regnum coelorum, obstrinxit fidem ad Baptismi necessitatem. Itaque omnes exinde credentes tinguebantur. Tunc et Paulus ubi credidit, tinctus est. Et hoc est quod Dominus in illa plaga orbationis praeceperat: Exsurge, dicens, et introi Damascum, illic tibi demonstrabitur quid debeas agere, scilicet tingui, quod solum ei deerat. Alioquin satis didicerat atque crediderat Nazarenum esse Dominum Dei Filium.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, those most wicked ones provoke these questions. So, they say, Baptism is not necessary for those for whom faith is enough, for even Abraham pleased God by the sacrament of faith, without any water. But in all things, later things conclude and following things prevail over preceding ones. Salvation was able to be in the past through bare faith before the Lord's passion and resurrection. But when faith was increased by believing in His birth, passion, and resurrection, an amplification of the sacrament was added, a sealing of Baptism, a kind of garment of faith, which was previously bare and did not have power without its own law. For the law of baptizing was imposed and a form was prescribed. Go, He says, teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. To this law, that definition was added: Unless someone is born again of water and Spirit, he will not enter into the kingdom of heaven, which bound faith to the necessity of Baptism. And so, from then on, all believers were baptized. Then also Paul, when he believed, was baptized. And this is what the Lord commanded in that stroke of blindness: Arise, He says, and enter into Damascus, there it will be shown to you what you ought to do, namely to be baptized, which alone was lacking to him. Otherwise, he had learned enough and had believed that the Nazarene is the Lord, the Son of God.

pass_b_english: So those utterly wicked characters are stirring up these questions. They claim baptism isn't necessary for people who have faith, since Abraham pleased God through the sacrament of faith alone, without any water at all. But they're arguing backward: in every case, what comes later decides the matter, and the subsequent overrides the prior. Before the Lord's passion and resurrection, salvation was possible through bare faith. But once faith expanded to include belief in his birth, passion, and resurrection, the sacrament was amplified — baptism was added as a seal, a kind of garment for faith that had previously stood naked and lacked power without its own governing law. That law of baptizing was imposed, and the form was prescribed: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19). To that law this definition was appended: "Unless someone is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven" (John 3:5) — which bound faith to the necessity of baptism. From that point on, every believer was baptized. Even Paul, the moment he believed, was baptized. That's exactly what the Lord commanded in that stroke of blindness: "Get up, go into Damascus, and there you will be told what you must do" — namely, be baptized, the one thing he still lacked. He had already learned and believed thoroughly that the Nazarene is the Lord, the Son of God.
